paper_topic: Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) reward for RLVR code generation under finite-sample uncertainty

nodes.text: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training large language models on tasks with automatic verification.
In code generation, unit tests provide a natural verifier: a solution is correct if it passes all tests.

This approach has driven significant advances, from early work on CodeRL (Le et al., 2022) and RLTF (Liu et al., 2023) to recent breakthroughs like DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) and DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024), which demonstrate that RL with verifiable rewards can substantially improve reasoning capabilities.
However, a fundamental challenge arises when computational constraints limit the number of unit tests executed per rollout.
The standard approach uses the pass-rate—the fraction of tests passed—as the reward signal.
When only m tests are executed (e.g., m = 5 for efficiency), this point estimate has high variance and can mislead the policy.
nodes.display_label: Pass-rate has high variance at small m

nodes.text: A solution that passes 4 out of 5 tests might receive a reward of 0.8, yet its true pass probability could plausibly range from 0.5 to 1.0.

This finite-sample noise creates a systematic failure mode: solutions that happen to pass a favorable subset of tests receive inflated rewards, potentially leading the policy to over-optimize noisy estimates rather than true code quality.
We propose the Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) reward, which addresses this challenge through principled uncertainty quantification.
Instead of treating the pass-rate as a point estimate, we model test outcomes as Bernoulli trials with unknown success probability and place a Beta prior over this probability.
After observing npass successes out of m tests, we compute the δ-quantile of the Beta posterior as the reward.
nodes.display_label: δ-quantile of Beta posterior as reward

nodes.text: This provides a conservative estimate that naturally penalizes solutions with high uncertainty: a solution passing 3/5 tests receives a lower LCB reward than one passing 27/30 tests, even though both have the same pass-rate of 0.6.
We propose the LCB reward for unit-test RLVR, which uses the lower confidence bound of a Beta posterior to account for finite-sample uncertainty in pass-rate estimation.
We demonstrate that LCB (m=5) achieves state-of-the-art Pass@1 accuracy on MBPP+ (57.0%) and HumanEval+ (57.1%), outperforming Pass-rate (2m=10) while using only half the verifier compute.
We show that LCB is robust to hyperparameter choices (δ, prior) and exhibits the most stable training dynamics among all tested reward functions.

observations: FA0008 follows a classic problem-solution arc with a single linear spine. The intro opens with two Context nodes establishing RLVR and unit-test verification (N1-N2), then anchors prior practice with a multi-citation Prior_Work cluster (N3, 4 citations). A 'However' marker pivots into N4, which is field-level problem framing (compute constraints on unit-test execution) and stays in Context. The pass-rate reward (N5) is then introduced as the standard Prior_Work, and only after that does the Limitation chain (N6-N8) begin: high variance at small m, the concrete 4/5 example, and the systematic over-optimization failure mode -- each is an explicit critique of the named pass-rate baseline. The Method block (N9-N12) is presented as a tightly nested elaboration chain (propose LCB → Bernoulli/Beta model → δ-quantile formula → conservative interpretation), with no internal forks. Three Contributions (C1-C3) receive 'addresses' edges from the limitation chain: N9 → N8 (LCB addresses the failure mode), N12 → N7 (the conservative estimate addresses the 4/5 example), N11 → N6 (the δ-quantile addresses high variance at small m). No competing-hypothesis fork; no anchor paper (this is a methodological extension rather than a single-paper follow-up).
